1:
Robertson takes the opening formula for a sign that this was among the items asked about in the letter to Paul, introduced just as the problem of meats offered to idols had been; the question runs to the end of the fourteenth chapter. Gill observes that the word gifts is not in the original text, though rightly supplied: the apostle means neither graces nor doctrines nor spiritual men, since spiritual gifts are the subject of this chapter and the two following. Clarke would as readily translate the words concerning spiritual persons as concerning spiritual gifts, and thinks the former agrees better with the context; what he wishes them to know is whence such gifts come and for what end, that each may serve the church in the capacity God has placed him in, so that there be no schism in the body. Ellicott sets the scene: in that early age the church was full of the divine energy of spiritual youth, and from the indwelling Spirit resulted marvellous gifts, some of which ceased with the apostolic age, some of which seem to have lingered for centuries, even to our own day, declaring themselves in times of profound religious awakening.

Chrysostom warns that this whole place is very obscure, but locates the obscurity in ourselves: it comes of our ignorance of the facts referred to, and of their cessation, being such as then occurred but now take place no longer. Whoever was baptized straightway spake with tongues, and not with tongues only, for many also prophesied; since on their coming over from idols, without any clear knowledge or training in the ancient Scriptures, they at once received the Spirit on their baptism, yet the Spirit they saw not, for it is invisible, and therefore God's grace bestowed some sensible proof of that energy. One spake straightway in the Persian, another in the Roman, another in the Indian, which made manifest to them without that it is the Spirit in the very person speaking. But most abundant of all was the gift of tongues, which became a cause of division — not from its own nature, Chrysostom is careful to say, but from the perverseness of those that had received it, the possessors of the greater gifts being lifted up against them that had the lesser, and these again envying the owners of the greater.

Henry draws the distinction on which the whole chapter turns. Gifts and graces greatly differ: both were freely given of God, but grace is given for the salvation of those who have it, whereas gifts are bestowed for the advantage and salvation of others; and there may be great gifts where there is not a dram of grace, the persons possessed of them being utterly out of the divine favour. They are great instances of divine benignity, but do not by themselves prove those who have them objects of divine complacency — this church was rich in gifts, yet many things were scandalously out of order in it. Barnes finds the abuse one of precedency, those thus favoured claiming higher honour than the less distinguished; he answers that all filled important places, as the parts of the human system are necessary to its symmetry and health. Calvin states the purpose the apostle will argue from. The Corinthians abused God's gifts for ostentation and show, and love was little regarded, so he shows for what purpose believers are adorned with them — for the edification of their brethren. That God is their author he proves from their own experience, reminding them how ignorant and stupid they were, and destitute of all spiritual light, before God called them, whence it appears they were furnished not by nature but through his unmerited benignity. Wesley notes that the abundance of these gifts in the churches of Greece refuted the idle learning of the Greek philosophers, though the Corinthians used them unwisely.
2:
Gill takes the word Gentiles here of religion rather than nation, the Syriac rendering it profane; and it must be understood of one part of the church only, since some were Jews. The apostle observes it to humble them, so that if they were now favoured with any of the Spirit's gifts these must be owing to grace and not to their deserts. Clarke says they were hurried by their passions into a senseless worship calculated only to gratify animal propensities; and the dumbness was double, for not only could the image not speak, but neither could the god or demon it pretended to represent — a full proof that an idol is nothing in the world. Barnes generalises sharply: no system of paganism consults the freedom and independence of the mind of man, but is everywhere a system of power and not of thought, its arrangements made to secure that power without an intelligent assent of the heart. Wesley puts it in a phrase, the blind carried away to the dumb, and that by the subtlety of their priests; Robertson notes the idiom of repetition in the last clause, as often as ye were led.

Ellicott finds the argument to lie in a comparison of miracles: so far from tongues and prophesying being the most wonderful, the greatest of all was their own conversion — that blind followers of dumb idols should be transformed into intelligent believers in the living Word was the most striking work of the Spirit, and they were no longer led hither and thither by diverse teachings, but had an unchanging principle of life. Barnes is careful about the second half of the rule that follows: the meaning is not that no one has the physical ability to say Jesus is Lord, since all men can say this, but that none will be heartily disposed to say it unless brought to that state by the Spirit. Clarke sets the rule in its setting: it was granted on all hands that there could be no religion without divine inspiration, and since the Spirit through all the law and the prophets gave testimony to the Messiah, no man under that inspiration could say to him anathema, as the Jews did; therefore, Clarke concludes, the Jews were no longer under the Spirit's inspiration. Wesley reduces the whole to a sum: none have the Holy Spirit but Christians, and all Christians have him.

Robertson hears in the confession a challenge to the empire. The word for Lord is common in the Greek Old Testament for God, and the Romans used it freely of the emperor in his worship; Deissmann calls the early establishment of a polemical parallelism between the cult of Christ and the cult of Caesar the most important thing of all, one inscription having Nero Lord quite as a formula, without the article, just as the Lord Jesus stands here. He is reminded of the demand made of Polycarp that he say Caesar is Lord, and how each time he replied Jesus is Lord, paying for his loyalty with his life. Lighthearted men today can say Lord Jesus flippantly or even irreverently, Robertson adds, but no Jew or Gentile then said it who did not mean it. Calvin draws the doctrine out of the experience: we must be directed by the Spirit of God, or we shall wander on for ever, and it follows that all things pertaining to the true knowledge of God are the gifts of the Holy Spirit. He raises the objection himself: since the wicked sometimes speak of Christ in honourable and magnificent terms, does this show they have the Spirit of God? He answers that they undoubtedly have, so far as that effect goes, but that the gift of regeneration is one thing and the gift of bare intelligence, with which Judas himself was endowed when he preached the gospel, quite another.
4:
Gill reads the diversity as a rebuke to both parties at once. The gifts spring from the free grace and good pleasure of God, not from the merits of men, so that those with the largest share should not boast of them as acquired by themselves, and those with the smallest should be content and thankful; for though the gifts differ, and none have all, yet all have some. Robertson notes that the word rendered diversities is an old term for distinctions or distributions, found only here in the New Testament, and that the word for gift means a favour bestowed without any merit. Clarke defines them as gracious endowments leading to miraculous results, by the extraordinary influences of the Holy Spirit; and on the second clause he lists the offices — apostle, prophet and teacher, under which were probably included bishop, pastor and deacon — the qualifications and the appointments alike coming immediately from the one Lord Jesus Christ. Wesley states the relation of the three verses in a figure: divers streams, but all from one fountain — this verse speaking of the Holy Ghost, the next of Christ, the sixth of God the Father.

Barnes draws out what the repetition is for. Since all these endowments are produced by the same Spirit, have the same divine origin, and answer some important purpose in the church, none is to be despised, nor any man authorised to treat another with contempt; the Spirit has divided and conferred them according to his sovereign will. The same follows for the offices: since all had their appointment from Christ, and all are necessary, none should be proud of an elevated station, nor depressed at being designated to a humbler one. Barnes defends the plain sense of the word Spirit against the German critics, at whose head he places Eichhorn, who would take it to mean nature, the same natural endowments cultivated in various measures by art and education. That reading, he says, makes manifest nonsense and is contrary to the whole scope of the passage; it destroys the concinnity of these three verses, in which the agency of the Spirit is recognised, then that of the Son, then that of the Father, presenting a connected view of the operations of all three in the work of redemption.

Calvin puts the matter as a question of proportion. The symmetry of the Church consists, so to speak, of a manifold unity, that is, when the variety of gifts is directed to one object, as in music there are different sounds, yet suited to each other with such an adaptation as to produce concord; it is therefore befitting that there be a distinction of gifts as well as of offices, and yet that all harmonise in one. He sets this passage beside the twelfth of Romans and finds the two doing opposite work. There he orders every one to be content with his own gifts and cultivate the department assigned him, prohibiting a foolish ambition that goes beyond its limits; here he orders every one to bring what he has to the common heap, and not keep back God's gifts so as to enjoy them apart, but to aim unitedly at the edification of all. The sum is that gifts are not distributed thus variously in order to be used apart, but that in the very division there is a unity, since one Spirit is the source of all, one God the Lord of all administrations and the author of all exercises of power. Calvin marks a further use of the passage, against those who think the name Spirit means nothing essential but merely the gifts or actions of divine power: Paul plainly testifies that there is an essential power of God whence all his works proceed, it being the office of the Spirit to put forth that power by conferring these gifts on men.
7:
Gill turns the phrase round: it is not that which the Spirit manifests, such as the grace of God or the doctrines of the gospel, but that which shows that a man has the Spirit — the gifts, ordinary or extraordinary, being such as declare their author. Barnes takes the word for that which makes anything conspicuous or plain, as conduct manifests the state of the heart: all the Spirit produces in the mind declares his character and work, as the works of God in the visible creation declare his perfections. He is careful about the reach of the every man. The apostle is discoursing only of Christians, and the verse is very improperly adduced to prove that the gifts of the Holy Spirit are conferred alike on all men, or that pagans and blasphemers are under his enlightening influences; it means simply that the Spirit gives each Christian such graces as he pleases, distributing them not equally but as he chooses. Robertson notes that the word is late, occurring in the New Testament only here and in the second epistle to Corinth.

On the purpose of it the commentators are of one mind. Clarke reports that the fathers render the word variously, by illumination, by demonstration, by operation, and takes the apostle's meaning to be that whatever gifts God has bestowed, and in whatever ways the Spirit may have shown himself, it is all for the common benefit of the church: God has given no gift to any man for his own private advantage, but for the benefit of others as well as for his own salvation. Ellicott presses the word itself to the same end: if the gift were only for a man's own benefit it would cease to be a showing forth at all, since it would be enough to possess the Spirit consciously to oneself; but the object of light is to give light to others, and the object of the spiritual light is to make it plain to others. Calvin says the apostle points out the purpose for which God has appointed his gifts, since he does not confer them in vain, nor intend them to serve the purpose of ostentation. He allows the word two senses, passive and active, and prefers the active: the Spirit, when he enriches us with any gift, unlocks his treasures to bring out things that would otherwise have been concealed and shut up. A third view he rejects as harsh and forced, that the term is used because unbelievers recognise God only by visible miracles. Wesley states it in a line: the gift whereby the Spirit manifests itself, given to each for the profit of the whole body.

Barnes warns against reading the list that follows as a ranking. It is not certain that the apostle meant wisdom for the most elevated endowment because he places it first, since his design seems not to observe the order of value, but to state, as it occurred to him, that these various endowments had been conferred on different men. One man will be distinguished as a wise and prudent counsellor, another for knowledge, having a clear view of the plan of salvation and of the duties of religion; and the same variety is observed in the ministry at all times, both being equally useful in their place. All is to be traced to the same Spirit, Barnes adds, so that neither should pride himself in his endowments above the other. Clarke would render the word before each gift not word but doctrine, as in many other places of the New Testament, and takes the doctrine of wisdom for the mystery of our redemption, in which the wisdom of God was most eminently conspicuous — that of which Christ is the great teacher, himself called the wisdom of God, in whom are contained all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
9:
On the faith named here all agree it is not the saving kind. Ellicott says it cannot mean the faith necessary to salvation, since that belongs to all Christians; Robertson calls it not the faith of surrender but wonder-working faith; Wesley takes it for an extraordinary trust in God under the most dangerous circumstances. Gill would rather have it the doctrine of faith, with ability to preach it and boldness to defend it in the face of all opposition, given more or less to pastors and teachers, though he grants it is generally understood of a faith of working miracles. Barnes uses the word to praise a quality he thinks undervalued: many of the most useful men in the church are distinguished mainly for their simple confidence in God's promises, and often accomplish more by prayer and faith than others who are distinguished for wisdom and learning. Faith is one of the highest endowments of the Christian life, and yet one of the rarest; perhaps by many it is despised because it may be obtained by all, and is a grace in which the poor and humble may be as much distinguished as the man of splendid talents.

Wesley will not confine the gift of healing to its most conspicuous form. It need not be wholly restricted to healing diseases with a word or a touch, for it may exert itself also, though in a lower degree, where natural remedies are applied, and it may often be this, and not superior skill, which makes some physicians more successful than others. He gives the principle a figure: as, after the golden shields were lost, the king of Judah put brazen ones in their place, so, after the pure gifts were lost, the power of God exerts itself in a more covert manner, under human studies and helps. Gill reports a second reading of the working of miracles, that some understand the extraordinary powers the apostles had of punishing offenders, instancing Peter striking Ananias and Sapphira dead, Paul smiting Elymas with blindness, and the delivering of the incestuous person to Satan. Ellicott warns that prophecy is not to be taken in its modern limited sense of foretelling the future, but of forthtelling truth generally. On the discerning of spirits Barnes explains why it was needed: where the gift of prophecy was possessed, and conferred such advantages, there would be many pretenders to it, and it was of vast importance to the infant church that there be a power of detecting the imposture. Robertson calls it a most needed gift, to tell whether the gifts were really of the Holy Spirit — or, he adds, the so-called gifts of today — or merely strange though natural, or even diabolical.

Clarke observes that all these gifts were miraculously bestowed and could not be acquired by human art, the different languages excepted, and that even these were given in such circumstances as sufficiently proved them miraculous also. Wesley notes that the words as he will imply not so much arbitrary pleasure as a determination founded on wise counsel. Calvin draws the conclusion the list has been building towards. Those act amiss who, having no concern for participation, break asunder that holy harmony which is fitly adjusted only when, under the guidance of the same Spirit, all conspire toward one object. The apostle calls them back to unity by reminding them that all have derived from one fountain whatever they possess, and that no one has so much as to have enough within himself, so as not to require help from others; to no one does the Spirit give all, lest any, satisfied with his own portion, should separate himself from the rest and live solely for himself. And since will is here ascribed to the Spirit, and that in connection with power, Calvin concludes the Spirit to be truly and properly God.
12:
Chrysostom notices the apostle's habit of reasoning from nature, as when he asked whether nature does not teach that long hair is a dishonour to a man and a glory to a woman, and when, forbidding the idol-sacrifices, he drew his arguments from the Olympic games, from shepherds and soldiers and husbandmen. Here he brings forward another common example, by which he fights hard to prove that no one was really put in a worse condition — a thing marvellous to be able to demonstrate, and calculated to refresh the weaker sort. For nothing so consoles the person of small spirit and inferior gifts, Chrysostom says, or so persuades him not to grieve, as being convinced that he is not left with less than his share. Gill states the ground plainly: a human body is but one, and not more. Clarke fills it out: though the human frame has many members and a great variety of parts, it is yet one entire system, every part being requisite to the completeness of the whole.

On the abruptness of the second clause they divide over what is meant. Clarke observes that it cannot be supposed Christ is composed of many members, so that the term Church must be supplied — unless, which he thinks not improbable, the name Christ is here used to express the church, or whole company of Christian believers. Barnes reaches it by a figure of speech: as the head is the most important part it may stand for the whole, and the name Christ, the head of the church, is here put for the whole of which he is head, a figure common in all languages. Robertson grants that one would naturally expect the apostle to say, so also is the body of Christ, and notes that Aristotle had used the word body of the state, the body politic; what Paul means is that Christ as head has a body composed of members with varied gifts and functions, like the parts of the human frame, all vitally joined to the head and to each other. Calvin recalls that Menenius Agrippa, when he wished to conciliate the Roman people at variance with the senate, made use of an apologue not very unlike the doctrine of Paul here; and adds that the gifts were not conferred that every one should enjoy his own separately, but that one should help another.

Henry expounds the similitude at length. Christ and his church make one body, as head and limbs, made up of many parts yet but one, since all are baptized into it and made to drink of the same Spirit; Jews and Gentiles, bond and free, are upon a level in this. Christians are enrolled by baptism, the outward rite being of divine institution, significant of the new birth and therefore called the washing of regeneration; but it is by the renewing of the Holy Ghost that we are grafted in, and not merely by drinking the wine at the other ordinance but by drinking into one Spirit that we are maintained in union with him. Being animated by one Spirit is what knits Christians into one. He then turns it to the comfort of the least. The lowliest member makes a part of the whole, and though the foot and the ear are less useful, perhaps, than the hand and the eye, they do not cease to belong to it; so the meanest in Christ's body stands as truly there as the noblest, and is as dearly cherished. And the variety is not a defect but a beauty: were the whole an eye, where were the hearing? and what a monster would a frame be if it were all ear, or eye, or arm! It is therefore for the beauty of the church that there should be diversity of gifts and offices in it.
13:
What the baptism here means divides them. Gill denies flatly that water is intended, since the apostle says not in one and the same water but by one Spirit; not all who are washed are baptized by the Spirit, as the case of Simon Magus shows, and the outward rite does not of itself incorporate anyone into the church, seeing that persons may receive it and yet never be joined to one. There is an allusion to it, he grants, but what is intended is the grace of the Spirit in regeneration and sanctification. Barnes agrees that the connexion seems rather to require the baptism of the Holy Ghost, though Bloomfield, Calvin and Doddridge understand the ordinance, in which case the sense would be that by the very profession then made they had all become members of one and the same body. Calvin takes it as a proof drawn from the effect of the rite: we are by it engrafted into Christ's body, bound together as members by a mutual link and living one life, and every one who would remain in the church must therefore cultivate this fellowship. He speaks, however, of the washing of believers, efficacious through the grace of the Spirit, for in many it is merely in the letter, the symbol without the reality; and lest anyone should imagine the thing effected by the outward sign, the apostle adds that it is the work of the Holy Spirit. Robertson reads it of a definite past event in the life of each, of whatever race or class, when they put on the outward badge of service to Christ, the token of an inward change already wrought in them.

Clarke draws the comparison out through the soul. As the body of man, though composed of many members, is informed and influenced by one soul, so the church of Christ, which is his body, is informed and influenced by one Spirit, the Holy Ghost actuating and working by his spiritual frame as the human soul does in ours. Wesley marks how far apart the pairs stand: Jews and Gentiles at the greatest distance by nature, slaves and freemen at the greatest distance by law and custom, and yet all united in one body. Barnes lingers on the second pair: religion conferred no favours on the free which it did not confer on the bondman, and this would tend to secure their proper treatment more than anything else could, while increasing rather than diminishing their real respect for their masters, if they regarded them as fellow Christians destined to the same heaven.

On the drinking they divide again. Barnes thinks it probably refers to their partaking together of the cup in the Lord's Supper, so that by drinking of one cup they had shared the same influences of the Holy Ghost. Calvin is of the same mind, and gives his reason: the apostle intended an allusion to the similitude of the sign, and there is no correspondence between drinking and washing, whereas in that ordinance we drink of the life-giving blood of Christ, that we may have life in common with him. Ellicott would render the clause not to drink into but simply to drink one Spirit, and takes the rite to have been not only a watering of the convert with the washing of regeneration but a partaking of one Spirit on his part, the verb being that used where Apollos watered. Robertson refers it rather to the inward experience which the rite symbolised. Clarke understands a being made partakers of the gifts and graces of the Holy Ghost, agreeably to the words of our Lord, that if any man thirst he should come and drink. Wesley combines the two: in that cup, received by faith, we all imbibed one Spirit, who first inspired, and still preserves, the life of God in our souls.
14:
Robertson allows that the opening statement sounds like a truism, but calls it the key to the whole problem of church life, local and general; and the parable behind it was an old one, Socrates having asked how absurd it would be if feet and hands worked against one another when God made them to co-operate, while Seneca and Marcus Aurelius allude to it too. Barnes tells the best-known version at length. It is the apologue used by Menenius Agrippa, as Livy relates, to repress a rebellion raised against the nobles as useless and cumbersome to the state: he represented the members of the body as conspiring against the stomach, on the ground that it was inactive and consumed everything, and showed that the consequence of the conspiracy the feet and hands and mouth entered into was a universal wasting away of the whole frame, for want of the nutriment the stomach supplied. The representation had the desired effect and quelled the rebellion. So, Barnes concludes, as the foot and the ear could not pretend to be no parts of the body merely because they were not the eye, no Christian, however humble his endowments, can pretend that he is useless because he is not more highly gifted. Robertson adds the short answer: thinking or saying so does not change the fact.

Ellicott finds the same idea turned into verse by Pope, and quotes it: what if the foot, ordained the dust to tread, or hand, to toil, aspired to be the head? what if the head, the eye, or ear declined to serve mere engines to the ruling mind? Just as absurd for any part to claim to be another in this general frame; just as absurd to mourn the fate the great directing Mind of all ordains; all are but parts of one stupendous whole, whose body Nature is, and God the soul. Gill gives the foot its dignity: it is the lowest member, nearest the earth, treading upon it, sustaining the whole weight of the body, and performing the more drudging exercises of standing and walking, and may represent one in the lowest station in the church, a doorkeeper in the house of God, with the smallest degree of heavenly affection and spiritual light. Clarke states the dependence plainly: as all the members of the body depend on each other, and minister to the general support of the system, so in the church the private members are intimately connected among themselves and with their pastors, without which union no church can subsist.

Wesley notices whom each complainant is made to envy. The foot is elegantly introduced as speaking of the hand, and the ear of the eye, each of a part that has some resemblance to it; so among men each is apt to compare himself with those whose gifts resemble his own, rather than with those at a distance, above or beneath him. He offers a reading of the four: perhaps the foot represents private Christians, the hand officers in the church, the eye teachers, the ear hearers. Calvin presses the absurdity of the supposed revolt. Each member ought to rest satisfied with its own place and not envy the others; if our hands were, from envy, to refuse to discharge their office, would nature endure it, and would the hand be listened to when wishing to be separated from the body? These things are said of the natural body, Calvin adds, but must be applied to the Church, lest ambition or misdirected emulation lead one who occupies an inferior station to grudge his services to those above him. Ellicott states the principle: it would be as absurd for the body to be one member as for the members to lose their individuality, since there is a corporate body composed of divers members — the difference between a dead machine and a living organism.
18:
Gill notes that the members of a natural body, as they are made and fashioned by God in the form they have, are each also set by him in the place they occupy. Barnes puts the reason: God has formed the body, with its various members, as he saw would best conduce to the harmony and usefulness of all. Robertson reads the opening words as marking the turn of the argument — but now, as things actually are, in contrast to that absurdity — and observes that the verb is middle, so that God did it, and of himself; why then, he asks, challenge God's will? Wesley adds only that it pleased him with the most exquisite wisdom and goodness. Calvin makes the appointment itself the argument. It has pleased God that the body should consist of various members, endowed with various offices and gifts; that member, therefore, which will not rest satisfied with its own station will wage war with God after the manner of the giants. Let us rather be subject to the arrangement God has appointed, Calvin says, that we may not to no purpose resist his will.

On the supposition that all were one member, Barnes states the consequence flatly: if there were nothing but an eye, an ear or a limb, there would be no body at all. So in the church, if there were none but apostles, or none but prophets and teachers, or none but those who spoke with tongues and could interpret them, it could not exist; a variety of talents in their proper places is as useful as are the various members of the human frame. Calvin gives the reason behind the arrangement: God has not acted at random in assigning different gifts to the members, but because it was necessary for the preservation of the body, since if this symmetry were taken away there would be utter confusion and derangement. He presses the apostle's word, which he takes for a mass all of one shape, not distinguished by any variety; for if God were to fashion our body into a mass of that kind it would be a useless heap. Robertson notes that the apostle is applying the logic of the previous verse to any member whatever, and that the application to the church is obvious — particularly pertinent, he adds, in the case of a church boss.

Ellicott marks the turn from the argument to the fact. From the reduction to absurdity of the previous verses the apostle comes to things as they are, and states that there is a mutual interdependence among the members, the eye being dependent on the hand and the head upon the feet; the illustration is drawn out in this direction, Ellicott suggests, to rebuke those who, possessing what were reckoned the important spiritual gifts, despised those the Spirit had bestowed on others. Gill observes that they are of different make and shape, in different parts and places, and of different use and service. Robertson calls the closing clause the argument in a nutshell, in a single epigram: many members, but one body. Wesley draws from that unity what he takes to be its necessary consequence, that the several members need one another. Calvin explains why the apostle repeats the point so often, and finds the stress of the whole question to lie here: the unity of the body is of such a nature as cannot be maintained but by a diversity of members, and while these differ from each other in offices and functions, it is in such a way as to have a mutual connection for the preservation of the one body. Hence no body can retain its standing without a diversified symmetry; and hence too, Calvin concludes, we may know to consult the public advantage as well as our own, by discharging, every one, the duty of his own station.
21:
Chrysostom marks the turn in the argument. Having checked the envy of those in lower rank, and taken off the dejection they were likely to feel because richer endowments had been vouchsafed to others, the apostle now humbles the pride of the highly favoured. Though a gift be smaller, yet is it necessary; and as when the one is absent many functions are impeded, so without the other there is a maim in the fulness of the Church. Chrysostom presses the exact words: he said not, will not say, but cannot say, so that even should it wish to, and actually pronounce the sentence, the thing remains out of the question and inconsistent with nature. He notices too the choice of instances, that Paul seizes the two extremes and tries his argument first on the hand and the eye, then on the head and the feet, so adding force to the example. Robertson compresses the whole into a phrase: the superior organs need the inferior ones.

Calvin sets the two halves of the exhortation side by side. Hitherto the apostle has shown what belongs to the office of the humbler members, to discharge their duty toward the whole and not grudge the more distinguished their eminence; now, turning about, he lays it upon the honoured not to look down on those beneath, whom they cannot do without. The eye excels the hand, and yet may neither scorn it nor insult over it as a thing superfluous; the argument Calvin traces here is drawn from usefulness, that whatever ranks lowest in general esteem proves the more indispensable, so that for the very safety of the frame such parts must never be held cheap. Gill observes that the apostle advances by a beautiful gradation, singling out the portions which are weaker, less creditable and less comely, and demonstrating how needful they are. Clarke identifies these feebler members with the principal viscera — heart, lungs, stomach and intestinal canal. A man may lose an eye by accident, an arm or a leg may be amputated, and he lives and remains vigorous; let stomach, heart or lungs be taken away and life becomes necessarily extinct. Hence, Clarke remarks, such organs are not merely covered, but the cavities lodging them are girded about and fortified for their defence. Wesley thinks rather of a more delicate and tender structure, the brains and bowels, or the veins, arteries and other minute channels.

Barnes turns the anatomy upon the church, and reckons the thought a beautiful one. Those members most retiring and feeble in appearance, hidden from public view, unnoticed and unknown — the lowly, the meek, the peaceable and the prayerful — are often more requisite to her true welfare than any celebrated for talent and learning. She can better spare many a man, even in the ministry, who is learned and eloquent and popular, than some obscure Christian who is to her what the heart and the lungs are to the life. Ellicott adds the plain sense of the following clause: the parts reckoned less seemly are the more abundantly cared for, being carefully clothed, as distinguished from the face and hands, which go uncovered. Barnes explains that the abundant honour spoken of is precisely a matter of apparel; what decency bids us conceal we not only cover but study to adorn, while the comely face is left bare. Robertson notes that the verb means literally to place around, as one puts on a garland or a garment, and that a word for gracefulness found nowhere else in the New Testament carries the point. Calvin supplies the reason: the dishonour of a single member turns out to the common disgrace of the whole body, and that is why we take such pains to cover what would shame us if seen.
24:
Ellicott begins with the punctuation: the clause about our comely parts closes the previous sentence, and a new one opens at “But God hath tempered,” where the ordinary practice of covering the body is shown to agree with God's evident intention. Gill takes the comely parts to be face, eyes, nose, lips and cheeks, which want no external covering nor any borrowed ornament; and so, he adds, those eminent for grace and holiness, holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience, need no such veil as the others to hide them from the world. Barnes reads the verb literally as mingled: God has made the parts coalesce, formed a strict union, made one dependent upon another and necessary to the harmony of the rest. Robertson finds the word rarer than that. Plato had used this very verb of the way God compounded the elements in creating soul and body; Paul, borrowing it, rejects the notion that matter is evil and the organs degrading, and paints a noble picture of the frame planned to be the temple of God's Spirit — aimed at the Epicurean sensualists of Corinth.

Calvin sees the point of verse eighteen repeated more explicitly. God has appointed this symmetry with a view to the advantage of the whole, since on no other terms can it keep its footing. Whence comes it that every member is spontaneously concerned for the honour of a less comely one, and that all agree to conceal its shame? The inclination was implanted by God, for without it the frame would quickly fly apart; and where anyone assumes more than belongs to him, Calvin warns, the body is not merely shattered and the order of nature perverted, but the authority of God is openly set at naught. Wesley states the honour plainly: the lacking part is cared for and served by the noblest. Ellicott observes that the Corinthians turned their differences of gifts into an occasion of schism, exalting some and depreciating others, when the variety was designed, as in the human frame, to breed a mutual dependence that promotes unity. Clarke presses that watchfulness: so completely has God tempered the whole that not the smallest visible part can be removed without injuring the proportions and producing deformity. The eyes and ears keep guard for the general safety, set in the head like sentinels in a tower to perceive the first approach of a foe.

Then the sympathy. Robertson notes that the word for suffering together is a medical term in Hippocrates and Galen, and that Plato had said the body politic feels the hurt as the whole man feels a hurt finger; the rejoicing is happily as true, for one may tingle with gladness all over, thanks to the nervous system and the tie between mind and matter. Barnes will not have it reckoned mere sympathy. A disease left unarrested is carried by the blood through every part until life is destroyed, so that the injury of one is by natural connexion the injury of all; and though the church has no such physical bond, the union is no less close, nor the effect of one member's conduct upon the others less certain. Hence, he urges, when one is tempted or afflicted the rest should bear one another's burdens; when one is poor they should supply his want; when one is persecuted for righteousness they should make common cause with him. And when a member is favoured with remarkable talent or raised to a station of influence and uses it for Christ, the benefit is common property, which ought to repress envy at another's elevation. Clarke adds that whatever adorns or strengthens any single part gives a general pleasure to the whole man; Calvin, that nothing so promotes harmony as this community of interest, when each feels himself enriched by the prosperity of others and impoverished by their want.
27:
Chrysostom anticipates the objection. What is the example of the body to us, since the body is a slave to nature while our good deeds are of choice? The apostle therefore turns the figure upon their own concerns, signifying that we ought to have from deliberate agreement the same concord of design that the limbs have from nature. And if our body ought not to be divided, much less Christ's, and less by as much as grace is mightier than nature. Chrysostom then presses the added word, severally. Since the whole body was not the Corinthian church but the church in every part of the world, the apostle qualifies his phrase: the church among you is one portion of that body which is made up of all the churches; so that you must be at peace not with yourselves alone but with the whole church throughout the world, if indeed you are members of it. Robertson gives the same word its plain force — each has his own place and function. Calvin, however, thinks Chrysostom's reading forced, and prefers to refer the phrase back to the division of members already made, so that each is a member according as his portion and definite work have been assigned him.

Ellicott marks the place of the verse: here the foregoing illustration is applied in general terms, its detailed application following immediately after. Gill guards the term against mistake. This is not Christ's natural body, which the Father prepared for him and in which he bore our sins on the tree, offered up once for all; nor his sacramental body, the bread in the supper which represents it; but his body mystical, the church. Nor were the Corinthians that whole body, only a part, as every congregation is a part of the church universal — and Wesley says the same in a breath. Barnes keeps the anatomy in view: as all the limbs compose one frame under a common head, so Christ presides over the whole. Henry draws the practical inference. Each is a member of the body, not the body; each depends upon the rest and owes them care and concern. Mutual indifference, therefore, and much more contempt and hatred and envy and strife, are things unnatural in Christians, as unnatural as limbs of one frame having no regard for each other, or quarrelling among themselves. This, Henry says, is the whole scope of the argument: to put down the proud, vaunting and contentious spirit that their spiritual gifts had raised among the Corinthians.

Clarke applies it to the ministry. Every member is meant to be subservient to the rest, to mourn and rejoice with them, and each is necessary to the beauty, proportion, strength and perfection of the whole; not one useless, not one superfluous. Paul, Apollos and Cephas, with all their variety of gifts, serve alike for the perfecting of the saints; hence no teacher should be exalted above another or set against him. As the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of thee, so luminous Apollos cannot say to laborious Paul, I can build up and preserve the church without thee. The foot planted to bear the whole fabric, the hands that swing at liberty, the eye that takes in distant prospects, are equally serviceable and equally dependent. Clarke grants that fancy might match particular ministers to particular limbs, but judges such matching no part of the apostle's plan. Calvin closes on the same note: what any man has was given him for his brethren's edification, and must be brought forward rather than buried within himself or used as his own. Let the richly endowed not swell with pride, since nothing is so slight as to be useless, the least of the pious bearing fruit according to his slender capacity; and let the lowlier neither envy those above them nor withhold their duty.
28:
Gill notes that the apostle, having given the various gifts of the Spirit which qualify men for service, here enumerates the several offices and officers themselves. Barnes reads the verb strictly: God has appointed, constituted, ordained these various ranks, and the sequence marks honour and endowment. The apostles stand first, holding the highest authority and most signally qualified; prophets come second in point of gifts and importance, teachers third. Clarke sees here the same evident distinctions God has made among the members of the human frame, and unfolds each title from its roots. An apostle is one sent from place to place, designated immediately by Christ and despatched to preach the gospel to all mankind. A prophet is one who speaks beforehand, predicting things to come under divine inspiration, though the word is often applied to any who preach the gospel. A teacher instructs the people in the elements of religion and in their duty toward each other. Wesley sharpens the list: apostles plant the gospel among the heathen; prophets either foretell what is coming or speak by extraordinary inspiration; teachers precede even those who work miracles, and under these heads the evangelists and pastors of Ephesians are comprised.

Calvin fixes on the order itself, and thinks it should be carefully observed. The Lord never appointed ministers without first endowing them with the requisite gifts and qualifying them for their duty; the natural order is that gifts come before the office to be discharged. From this he draws a sharp inference. Those are fanatics, and actuated by an evil spirit, who thrust themselves into the church while destitute of the necessary qualifications — as many boast that they are under the Spirit's influence, and glory in a secret call from God, while remaining unlearned and utterly ignorant. Calvin also divides the list. Some offices named are perpetual, being necessary for the government of the church; others were temporary, appointed at the outset for founding it and raising up Christ's kingdom, and ceasing shortly after. To the second class belongs the apostleship: the Lord created apostles to spread the gospel throughout the whole world, assigning them no fixed limits or parishes but sending them as ambassadors among all nations and languages, whereas a pastor has no commission over the whole world but must take care of the flock committed to his charge. By prophet, Calvin understands not one who predicts, but an eminent interpreter of Scripture endowed with uncommon wisdom in discerning the present necessity of the church and speaking suitably to it.

Robertson watches the sentence break its own shape. Paul begins as though he would say some apostles, some prophets, then abandons the construction for first, second, then; and at miracles he shifts from the concrete to the abstract. Prophets, Robertson says, are forth-speakers for God, still needed if men will let the Spirit move them to utter the deep things of God; and it is a calamity when a preacher is no longer a teacher but only an exhorter. On the two new terms the voices converge and differ. Barnes notes that the word for helps occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and means aid or those who render it, perhaps the care of the poor and sick and orphans, perhaps those who attended the apostles as Priscilla and Aquila did; governments comes from steering a ship. Robertson guesses deacons for the one and bishops or elders for the other, and remarks the curiosity that these two offices, never specifically named, are the two that have survived. Clarke takes helps rather as the apostles' assistants, who baptized converts and went where they could not, the Levites being called helps of the priests; and he denies that governments means ruling power at all, taking it for a deep comprehensive mind, profoundly wise and prudent. Barnes and Wesley agree that no permanent offices are established here.
29:
The list turns into a string of questions, and Robertson notes that the Greek particle heading each of them expects a negative answer from every group in turn. Gill supplies that answer bluntly: no. Some are prophets, as distinct from apostles; some are teachers, as distinct from both; and some are neither. Clarke reads the whole series the same way — all are not apostles, all are not prophets — and finds in it the settled method of God, who has distributed his various gifts among various persons, each of whom is needed for the complete edification of the body of Christ. Robertson observes a small irregularity at the close: the question about interpreting is added here to the catalogue given a verse or two earlier, though it did stand in the fuller list near the beginning of the chapter.

Barnes will not let the questions be softened into a wish. They imply, with strong emphasis, that there could not be and ought not to be an even distribution of endowment. It was simply not the case that all were equal, or that all were qualified for the offices that others actually filled. Whether a man approves the arrangement or not, Barnes says, it remains a plain matter of fact: some were fitted for the apostolic office and others were not, some were furnished with prophetic gifts and others were not, some had the gift of healing, or the talent of speaking different languages, or of interpreting them, and others had none of these. Gill adds a practical instance from the second question. When such gifts of healing were still in being, they were not common property; the anointing with oil for the recovery of the sick was performed by the elders of the church, not by its ordinary members, and the sick were to send for them on that occasion.

Calvin heads off a misreading before drawing his conclusion. It may well have happened that one man was endowed with many gifts and sustained two of the offices enumerated, and there is no inconsistency in that. But the apostle's design is twofold. He shows first that no one possesses such fulness in everything as to have a sufficiency within himself and stand in no need of others; and second, that offices no less than gifts are so distributed that no single member constitutes the whole, but each contributing his own portion to the common advantage, they together make up one entire and perfect body. And Calvin names what all this is meant to destroy. Paul means here to take away every occasion of proud boasting, of base envyings, of haughtiness and contempt of the brethren, of malignity and ambition, and of everything of that nature.
31:
The verse can be read three ways, and Gill lays them out: as an assertion, ye do covet earnestly the best gifts, but I can show you something better; as a question, do ye zealously affect them and emulate one another in pursuit of them; or, as the translators have it, as an exhortation. Barnes reports the weight of opinion for the first. Doddridge urged that it would be a contradiction, after showing that these gifts are not at their own option and that no one ought to aspire above another, to undo the whole argument by inviting such rivalry; Locke and Macknight agreed, and the Syriac renders it, because you are zealous of the best gifts I will show you a more excellent way. Grotius preferred a third sense, that they should pray God for the most useful endowments. Barnes nevertheless keeps the imperative, judging that the connection demands it. Clarke inclines the other way, and thinks the affirmative reading likely, since there were certainly more contentions at Corinth about the gifts than about the graces of the Spirit. Wesley simply reads it so: ye covet earnestly the best gifts, and they are worth your pursuit, though few of you can attain them. Calvin holds the difference slight as to the sense.

What the best gifts are is a second question. Gill takes them to be not the highest and most extraordinary of those named, but the most useful and beneficial to the church — preaching above the rest. The Corinthians seemed most desirous of speaking with different tongues, yet the apostle proves at length that prophesying is preferable, as more serviceable and therefore more eligible. Calvin diagnoses the same fault: they aimed at show rather than usefulness, so that prophecy was neglected while languages sounded forth among them with great display and little profit. He is careful to add that Paul is not addressing individuals, as though wishing every man to aspire to prophecy or the teaching office, but recommending a general desire to promote edification, that they may apply themselves the more diligently to whatever builds up. Robertson notes that the apostle unhesitatingly ranks some spiritual gifts above others, and that the verb for zeal carries here its good sense, not the envy it bears elsewhere. Ellicott insists the argument is not meant to check ardour or damp enthusiasm; the Spirit divides as he wills, but he wills to give each the best gift that each desires and is capable of receiving, so that receptivity, born of earnest and practical desire, is the determining cause in every case.

Then comes the turn. Barnes admires the skill of it: the apostle did not denounce their zeal as wicked, nor say it was wrong to desire high endowments, nor try to crush the impulse, but regulated it by setting before them an endowment more valuable than all the rest, open to everyone, and such that in the very proportion it was gained it would quiet discontent and strife and ambition and produce order and peace and contentment with their own lot. That endowment is love. Ellicott adds that the more excellent way is not some gift to be sought instead of the others, but a more excellent manner of seeking them all: not striving after any one because it is highly esteemed or apparently useful or easily got, but letting love consecrate every struggle and every attainment. Clarke gives the warning underneath — a man may possess the best of all these gifts and still be deficient in what is essential to his salvation, if he is without that love; and Wesley says the same, that here is a gift which all may, yea must, attain or perish. Robertson presses the Greek: the phrase is superlative rather than comparative, a way beyond all comparison; and the chapter division here is poor, for the sentence belongs with what follows.
